'''Peter Michael Neumann''' [[Order of the British Empire|OBE]] (28 December 1940 – 18 December 2020)<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=Leddy|first=Dorothy|date=2020|title=M500 298|url=https://m500.org.uk/magazine/|page=21}}</ref> was a British mathematician. His fields of interest included the [[history of mathematics]] and [[Galois theory]].

== Biography ==
Born in December 1940, Neumann was a son of the German-born mathematicians [[Bernhard Neumann]] and [[Hanna Neumann]]. He gained a [[Bachelor of Arts|BA]] degree from [[The Queen's College, Oxford]] in 1963, and a [[Doctor of Philosophy|DPhil]] degree from the [[University of Oxford]] in 1966.<ref name=":0" /> On completing his doctorate, Neumann was named a [[Tutorial Fellow]] at the Queen's College, Oxford, and in 1967 he became a lecturer at the [[University of Oxford]].<ref>{{cite journal
 | last1 = Liebeck | first1 = Martin W.
 | last2 = Praeger | first2 = Cheryl E.
 | date = July 2022
 | doi = 10.1112/blms.12690
 | issue = 4
 | journal = Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society
 | pages = 1487–1514
 | publisher = Wiley
 | title = Peter Michael Neumann, 1940–2020
 | volume = 54}}</ref> His research work was in the field of [[group theory]]. In 1987, Neumann won the [[Lester R. Ford]] Award of the [[Mathematical Association of America]] for his review of [[Harold Edwards (mathematician)|Harold Edwards']] book ''Galois Theory''.<ref>[http://www.maa.org/awards/ford.html The Lester R. Ford Award], MAA, retrieved 2010-02-01.</ref><ref>{{cite journal|year=1986|title=Book Review of ''Galois Theory'' by Harold M. Edwards|url=http://www.maa.org/programs/maa-awards/writing-awards/book-review-of-galois-theory-by-harold-m-edwards|journal=Amer. Math. Monthly|volume=93|pages=407–411|doi=10.2307/2323619|jstor=2323619}}</ref>

He was the first Chairman of the [[United Kingdom Mathematics Trust]], from October 1996 to April 2004, succeeded by [[Bernard Silverman]].<ref>{{cite book|title=The UK Mathematics Trust Yearbook 2003–2004|publisher=United Kingdom Mathematics Trust|year=2004|isbn=0953682358}}</ref>

Neumann showed in 1997 that [[Alhazen's problem]] (reflecting a light ray off a spherical mirror to hit a target) cannot be solved with a [[straightedge and compass construction]]. Although the solution is a straightforward application of [[Galois theory]] it settles the constructibility of one of the last remaining geometric construction problems posed in antiquity.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Highfield|first=Roger|date=1 April 1997|title=Don solves the last puzzle left by ancient Greeks|url=http://www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/Obits2/Al-Haytham_Telegraph.html|journal=[[Electronic Telegraph]]|volume=676|accessdate=2012-11-19}}</ref>

In 2003, the [[London Mathematical Society]] awarded him the [[Senior Whitehead Prize]].<ref>{{cite web
|url=http://www.lms.ac.uk/activities/prizes_com/pastwinners.html#swhitehead
|title=List of Prizewinners
|publisher=[[London Mathematical Society]]
|accessdate=2007-07-08
|archive-date=17 December 2005
|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051217180519/http://www.lms.ac.uk/activities/prizes_com/pastwinners.html#swhitehead
|url-status=dead
}}</ref> He was appointed [[Officer of the Order of the British Empire]] (OBE) in the [[New Year Honours 2008|2008 New Year Honours]].<ref>{{cite web| url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/shared/bsp/hi/pdfs/29_12_07_hons_queen.pdf | title=Officers of the Order of the British Empire | work=[[BBC News]] | publisher=[[BBC]] | location=UK | pages=32 | accessdate=27 January 2010 }}</ref>

After retiring in 2008, he became an Emeritus Fellow at the Queen's College.

Neumann's work in the [[history of mathematics]] includes his 2011 publication ''The Mathematical Writings of Évariste Galois'', an English language book on the work of French mathematician [[Évariste Galois]] (1811–1832).<ref>{{cite book|last=Neumann|first=Peter M.|title=The Mathematical Writings of Évariste Galois|date=2011|publisher=[[European Mathematical Society]]|isbn=978-3037191040|series=Heritage of European Mathematics}}</ref> Neumann was a long-standing supporter of the [[British Society for the History of Mathematics]], whose [[British Society for the History of Mathematics#Neumann Prize|Neumann Prize]] is named in his honour.<ref>{{cite web|title=Neumann Prize|url=https://www.bshm.ac.uk/neumann-prize|access-date=2020-12-18|publisher=[[British Society for the History of Mathematics]]|location=UK}}</ref>

Neumann was the president of the [[Mathematical Association]] from 2015 to 2016.<ref name=":0" />

Neumann died from [[COVID-19]] on 18 December 2020, ten days before his 80th birthday, during the [[COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.lms.ac.uk/news-entry/21122020-0842/dr-peter-neumann-1940-2020|date=21 December 2020|accessdate=31 December 2020|title=Dr Peter Neumann (1940–2020)|work=News|publisher=London Mathematical Society}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/education/2021/jan/04/peter-neumann-obituary|title= Peter Neumann obituary |last=Neumann|first=David|work=The Guardian|date=4 January 2021|access-date=11 January 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://cameroncounts.wordpress.com/2020/12/18/peter-neumann/|website=Peter Cameron's blog|last=Cameron|first=Peter|authorlink=Peter Cameron (mathematician)|title=Peter Neumann|date=18 December 2020|accessdate=22 December 2020}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Neumann married Sylvia Bull in 1962. She was a fellow mathematics undergraduate at Oxford, where they met.<ref name=":1" />
